lessons.title: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
objectives: Distinguish defining relative clauses from non-defining clauses that add extra information.
Use commas and who/which correctly in non-defining relative clauses.
Recognize when an object relative pronoun can be omitted in a defining clause.

explanation.en:
### Core rule / Meaning Some relative clauses identify **which** person/thing we mean (*defining*). Others add extra information about an already identified person/thing (*non-defining*).

### When to use

| Type | Meaning | Punctuation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Defining** | Identifies the intended person/thing; information is needed to identify it | Normally no commas | The student **who won the prize** is in my class. |
| **Non-defining** | Gives extra information about someone/something already identified | Set the extra clause off with commas | My aunt, **who lives in Hue**, is visiting us. |

### Relative words and omission
- **who** refers to a person; **which** refers to a thing. In a **non-defining clause**, do **not** use **that** instead of **who/which**.
- In a **defining clause**, *that* may be possible for people or things in relevant contexts, subject to clause constraints.
- **Object relative pronoun** in a defining clause may sometimes be omitted: *The film (that) we watched was excellent* → *The film we watched was excellent*.
- **Subject relative pronoun** should not be omitted in that structure: *The student who won the prize...*; not *The student won the prize is...*.
- **Non-defining relative clause:** **Never omit the relative pronoun**, whether it functions as a subject or an object. The option to omit an object relative pronoun applies **only to defining clauses** (and only in the relevant grammatical environment).

### Worked examples
- *The student who won the prize is in my class.* → The clause tells us **which student**.
- *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us.* → The relative clause adds information about *my aunt*.
- *This camera, which I bought last year, still works well.* → **which** adds information about *this camera*; commas mark the extra clause.
- *The film we watched was excellent.* → Object relative pronoun is omitted in a defining clause.

### Common mistakes
- *My aunt, that lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✗ → *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✓ (non-defining clause: not **that**).
- *The student won the prize is in my class* ✗ → *The student who won the prize is in my class* ✓ (cannot omit subject relative pronoun there).
- Treat commas as **meaningful** in this lesson: do not assume defining and non-defining uses are interchangeable.

### Remember First ask whether the relative clause *identifies which one* or *adds extra information*. Then choose punctuation and pronoun accordingly. Never omit a relative pronoun in a non-defining clause; in a defining clause, only an object relative pronoun may sometimes be omitted.
explanation.vi: *Mệnh đề xác định giúp chỉ rõ người/vật và thường không có dấu phẩy; đôi khi có thể bỏ đại từ quan hệ làm tân ngữ. Mệnh đề không xác định chỉ bổ sung thông tin, có dấu phẩy, không dùng “that” và **không được lược bỏ đại từ quan hệ**.*

examples: DEFINING · The student who won the prize is in my class.
NON-DEFINING · My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us.
THING · This camera, which I bought last year, still works well.
OBJECT OMITTED · The film we watched was excellent.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a non-defining relative clause?

options.text: My uncle, who lives in Hue, is visiting us.
My uncle that lives in Hue is visiting us,
My uncle who, lives in Hue is visiting us.
My uncle, that lives in Hue, is visiting us.

feedback.explanation_en: The person is already identified as my uncle, so the extra information is set off by commas and who is used rather than that.

activities.prompt: Choose the sentence in which the relative clause identifies which student we mean.

options.text: The student who borrowed my pen is waiting outside.
Lan, who borrowed my pen, is waiting outside.
My teacher, who borrowed my pen, is waiting outside.
Mr Nam, who borrowed my pen, is waiting outside.

feedback.explanation_en: The defining clause who borrowed my pen identifies which student; it is essential information and has no commas.

activities.prompt: Which relative word is standard in this non-defining clause? My tablet, ___ I use for homework, is three years old.

feedback.explanation_en: Which is standard for a thing in a non-defining relative clause; that is not used in this pattern.

activities.prompt: Write the missing relative word: Mai, ___ won the science prize, is in my class.

feedback.explanation_en: Mai is already identified, so who introduces the non-defining clause about a person.

activities.prompt: Which defining relative clause correctly omits an object relative pronoun?

options.text: The book I borrowed was excellent.
The student won the prize is my friend.
The phone belongs to me is on the desk.
The teacher helps us is absent today.

feedback.explanation_en: In The book I borrowed, the omitted relative pronoun would be the object of borrowed. Subject relative pronouns cannot be omitted in the other examples.

activities.prompt: Which sentence needs the relative pronoun because it is the subject of the relative clause?

options.text: The girl who designed the poster is twelve.
The film that we watched was funny.
The book I bought is useful.
The game we played was difficult.

feedback.explanation_en: Who is the subject of designed and cannot be omitted.

activities.prompt: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

options.text: Our school library, which reopened in September, is much brighter now.
Our school library which, reopened in September is much brighter now.
Our school library, that reopened in September, is much brighter now.
Our school library which reopened, in September is much brighter now.

feedback.explanation_en: The extra information is a non-defining clause, so it is enclosed by commas and uses which.

activities.prompt: Write only the missing word: My laptop, ___ I bought last year, still works well.

feedback.explanation_en: The laptop is already identified and the clause is non-defining, so which is used; that is not standard here.

activities.prompt: What is the usual meaning of “The students who finished early left the room”?

options.text: Only the students who finished early are identified as leaving.
All the students finished early, and all left.
The sentence means exactly the same as one with commas.

feedback.explanation_en: Without commas, the defining clause identifies a particular group: the students who finished early.

activities.prompt: Combine the ideas as a non-defining clause: “Our art teacher is Ms Hoa. She studied in Paris.”

options.text: Our art teacher, who studied in Paris, is Ms Hoa.
Our art teacher that studied in Paris is Ms Hoa.
Our art teacher who, studied in Paris, is Ms Hoa.
Our art teacher, which studied in Paris, is Ms Hoa.

feedback.explanation_en: Who with commas correctly adds extra information about the already identified person.

lessons.title: Gerunds and infinitives after common verbs
objectives: Use -ing forms after common verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish and suggest.
Use to + infinitive after common verbs such as want, plan, decide and hope.
Choose the correct verb pattern without adding an unnecessary preposition or auxiliary.

explanation.en:
### Core rule / Meaning

Different verbs take different following patterns. Commonly **enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest** are followed by a **verb-ing** phrase; **want, plan, decide, hope** are commonly followed by **to + base verb**. Learn the pairings in their intended meanings rather than choosing freely.

### When to use + worked example + why
- **Enjoy an activity:** Ravi **enjoys designing** paper lanterns. → Enjoy is followed by -ing in this pattern.
- **Avoid an action:** We **avoid crossing** the busy street at lunchtime. → Avoid takes -ing here.
- **Finish an activity:** Lena **finished arranging** the flowers. → The following verb is an -ing form.
- **Plan and hope:** We **plan to organise** a class exhibition. / They **hope to win** a prize. → Plan and hope commonly take to + base verb.
- **Suggest an action:** Dad **suggested ordering** a pizza. → The following action takes -ing, not to-infinitive.

### form / formula / decision cues (adaptive)
- **Common -ing patterns:** **enjoy/avoid/finish/suggest + verb-ing**.
- **Common to-infinitive patterns:** **want/plan/decide/hope + to + base verb**.
- The choice is **verb-specific**; other verbs may allow both patterns, sometimes with changed meaning.

### common mistakes (review for accuracy and alternatives)
- ⚠️ *They **finished to clean** the kitchen.* → **They **finished cleaning** the kitchen.** (In this pattern, finish takes an -ing phrase.)
- ⚠️ *We **hope meeting** the illustrator.* → **We **hope to meet** the illustrator.** (Hope commonly takes a to-infinitive.)

### Remember / comparison (adaptive)

Remember the **first verb + next verb pattern** as a pair. Do not add extra to or -ing unless that verb permits it.
explanation.vi: Các động từ có mẫu theo sau khác nhau: enjoy/avoid/finish/suggest thường đi với -ing, còn want/plan/decide/hope thường đi với to + động từ nguyên mẫu. Nên học theo cặp động từ và mẫu, không tự thêm to/-ing tùy ý.

examples: I enjoy reading graphic novels.
Try to avoid using your phone during study time.
We plan to visit the museum on Saturday.
She decided to join the school club.

activities.prompt: I really enjoy ___ graphic novels.

feedback.explanation_en: Enjoy is followed by an -ing form: enjoy reading.

activities.prompt: We decided ___ the earlier bus.

feedback.explanation_en: Decide is followed by to + infinitive: decided to take.

activities.prompt: Try to avoid ___ your phone while you are studying.

feedback.explanation_en: Avoid is followed by an -ing form: avoid using.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence with the correct form of study: I plan ___ harder before the exam.

feedback.explanation_en: Plan is followed by to + infinitive: plan to study.

activities.prompt: She finished ___ her presentation just before lunch.

feedback.explanation_en: Finish is followed by an -ing form: finished preparing.

activities.prompt: They hope ___ the final next week.

feedback.explanation_en: Hope is followed by to + infinitive in this pattern: hope to reach.

activities.prompt: Complete with the correct form of write: He enjoys ___ short stories.

feedback.explanation_en: Enjoy is followed by the -ing form writing.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct verb pattern?

options.text: The teacher suggested taking a short break.
The teacher suggested to take a short break.
The teacher suggested take a short break.
The teacher suggested to taking a short break.

feedback.explanation_en: Suggest is normally followed by an -ing form in this pattern: suggested taking.

activities.prompt: Which pair is correct?

feedback.explanation_en: Avoid takes -ing and decide takes to + infinitive.

activities.prompt: Mina wants ___ her pronunciation before the presentation.

feedback.explanation_en: Want is followed by to + infinitive: wants to improve.

lessons.title: Indirect questions and question tags
objectives: Use statement word order after an indirect-question opener.
Use if or whether to introduce indirect yes/no questions.
Form common question tags by matching the auxiliary and reversing positive/negative polarity.

explanation.en:
### Core rule / Meaning

An **indirect question** asks more politely or embeds a question inside another sentence; its inner clause normally has **statement word order**, not direct-question inversion. For yes/no content use **if/whether**. A **question tag** checks or invites agreement after a statement and usually uses the matching auxiliary with opposite positive/negative polarity.

### When to use + worked example + why
- **Polite wh-question:** Could you explain **how this machine works**? → The embedded clause is subject then verb: this machine works.
- **Ask about a place:** I wonder **where the exhibition begins**. → There is no extra does inside the embedded clause.
- **Indirect yes/no question:** Do you know **whether the hall is accessible**? → Whether introduces the yes/no content.
- **Positive statement plus negative tag:** The garden looks beautiful, **doesn’t it**? → A present simple main verb uses does in a negative tag.
- **Negative statement plus positive tag:** They **weren’t** at the meeting, **were they**? → The past be auxiliary is reversed in the tag.

### form / formula / decision cues (adaptive)
- **Indirect wh-question:** opener + question word + **subject + verb**.
- **Indirect yes/no question:** opener + **if/whether + subject + verb**.
- **Usual tags:** positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag; match auxiliary, time and subject pronoun.

### common mistakes (review for accuracy and alternatives)
- ⚠️ *Could you tell me why **is** the gate locked?* → **Could you tell me why the gate **is** locked?** (Do not invert the inner indirect-question clause.)
- ⚠️ *They **aren’t** invited, **aren’t they**?* → **They **aren’t** invited, **are they**?** (A negative statement usually takes a positive tag.)

### Remember / comparison (adaptive)

For an **indirect question**, keep the inside clause in statement order. For a **tag**, check the auxiliary, polarity and pronoun.
explanation.vi: Câu hỏi gián tiếp dùng trật tự câu kể sau từ để hỏi, không đảo trợ động từ trong mệnh đề bên trong. Với câu hỏi yes/no, dùng if/whether. Câu hỏi đuôi thường đổi khẳng định/phủ định và dùng đúng trợ động từ, đại từ.

examples: Could you tell me where the station is?
Do you know what time the shop closes?
Do you know if the library is open?
She is your cousin, isn't she? · You don't live here, do you?

activities.prompt: Choose the correct indirect question.

options.text: Could you tell me where the library is?
Could you tell me where is the library?
Could you tell me where does the library be?
Could you tell me where the library does is?

feedback.explanation_en: After the indirect-question opener, use statement word order: where the library is.

activities.prompt: Do you know ___ the shop closes?

feedback.explanation_en: The indirect clause uses statement order: what time the shop closes.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct indirect yes/no question.

options.text: Do you know if the library is open?
Do you know is the library open?
Do you know does the library open?
Do you know if is the library open?

feedback.explanation_en: Use if or whether plus statement word order for an indirect yes/no question.

activities.prompt: Complete the indirect question: Could you tell me ___? (where / the station / be)

feedback.explanation_en: The indirect clause uses statement order: where the station is.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly removes direct-question inversion?

options.text: I'd like to know why the lesson ended early.
I'd like to know why did the lesson end early.
I'd like to know why ended the lesson early.
I'd like to know why does the lesson ended early.

feedback.explanation_en: An indirect wh-question uses statement word order and no do/did inversion.

activities.prompt: She is your cousin, ___?

feedback.explanation_en: A positive statement with is takes the negative matching tag isn't she.

activities.prompt: You don't live near here, ___?

feedback.explanation_en: A negative present-simple statement with don't takes the positive tag do you.

activities.prompt: He can swim well, ___?

feedback.explanation_en: A positive statement with can takes the negative matching tag can't he.

activities.prompt: They arrived early, ___?

feedback.explanation_en: A positive past-simple statement takes the negative tag with did: didn't they.

activities.prompt: We'll meet at six, ___?

feedback.explanation_en: A positive statement with will takes the negative matching tag won't we.

lessons.title: Word families for study and communication
objectives: Recognize common noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms in familiar word families.
Use suffix clues such as -tion, -ment, -ive and -ly to choose a form that fits a sentence.
Use word-family knowledge together with sentence meaning rather than relying on spelling alone.

explanation.en: At B1, useful vocabulary growth includes noticing how one base can form several related words: decide → decision, improve → improvement, communicate → communication, effective → effectively. The correct form depends on the grammar and meaning of the sentence. A noun may follow an article, an adjective may describe a noun, and an adverb may describe how an action happens. Suffixes are helpful clues, but always check the whole context.
explanation.vi: Ở mức B1, học từ vựng hiệu quả bằng cách nhận ra các từ cùng họ: decide → decision, improve → improvement, communicate → communication, effective → effectively. Dạng đúng phụ thuộc vào ngữ pháp và nghĩa của cả câu. Hậu tố là gợi ý hữu ích nhưng phải luôn kiểm tra ngữ cảnh.

examples: DECIDE → We made a difficult decision.
IMPROVE → I can see a clear improvement.
COMMUNICATE → Good communication helps a team.
EFFECTIVE → The group worked effectively.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct form: The team made an important ___ before the meeting ended.

feedback.explanation_en: After an important, a noun is needed; decision is the noun in this word family.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct form: Regular feedback can lead to a clear ___.

feedback.explanation_en: A clear requires a noun; improvement names the positive change.

activities.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence? Good ___ is especially important when a group works online.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence needs a noun naming the process of sharing information.

activities.prompt: Choose the best form: The students divided the work ___ and finished on time.

feedback.explanation_en: The blank describes how they divided the work, so the adverb effectively fits.

activities.prompt: In this sentence, what does 'reliable' most nearly mean? 'We need a reliable source before we include the fact in our report.'

feedback.explanation_en: A reliable source is one that can be trusted.

activities.prompt: Complete with the noun form of develop: The project showed steady ___ over three months.

feedback.explanation_en: Development is the noun form that fits after steady.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct form: Her explanation was clear and ___.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence coordinates two adjectives after was: clear and informative.

activities.prompt: Which word best fits? The instructions were so ___ that everyone completed the task correctly.

feedback.explanation_en: An adjective is needed after were so; helpful describes the instructions.

activities.prompt: Complete with the adverb form of careful: Please read the final paragraph ___.

feedback.explanation_en: Carefully is the adverb that describes how to read.

activities.prompt: Which pair belongs to the same word family and is used correctly?

feedback.explanation_en: Success is a noun and successful is the related adjective.

lessons.title: Collocations for plans, problems and decisions
objectives: Use common B1 collocations connected with plans, decisions and problem solving.
Distinguish natural verb–noun combinations from grammatically possible but unnatural combinations.
Infer the meaning of a collocation from a realistic sentence.

explanation.en: Fluent vocabulary use depends on combinations that commonly occur together. Useful B1 examples include make a decision, reach an agreement, solve a problem, meet a deadline, take responsibility, raise a concern and consider an option. Learning these as complete chunks helps both comprehension and production. When more than one verb seems possible, use the combination that is conventional in standard English.
explanation.vi: Dùng từ tự nhiên phụ thuộc nhiều vào các từ thường đi cùng nhau. Một số cụm B1 hữu ích là make a decision, reach an agreement, solve a problem, meet a deadline, take responsibility, raise a concern và consider an option. Nên học theo cả cụm thay vì từng từ riêng lẻ.

examples: We need to make a decision by Friday.
Both groups finally reached an agreement.
The team solved the problem before lunch.
She raised a concern about the new schedule.

activities.prompt: Which phrase is most natural?

feedback.explanation_en: Make a decision is the standard collocation.

activities.prompt: The two groups discussed the issue and finally ___ an agreement.

feedback.explanation_en: Reach an agreement is a standard collocation meaning come to a shared decision.

activities.prompt: We have only two days left, so everyone must work carefully to ___ the deadline.

feedback.explanation_en: Meet a deadline means complete the required work by the required time.

activities.prompt: Complete the collocation: We need to ___ this problem before the next lesson.

feedback.explanation_en: Solve a problem is the natural verb–noun combination.

activities.prompt: In 'Linh raised a concern about the cost,' what did Linh do?

feedback.explanation_en: Raise a concern means bring a worry or possible problem to attention.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses take responsibility naturally?

options.text: He took responsibility for checking the final file.
He made responsibility for checking the final file.
He did responsibility to the final file.
He reached responsibility for the final file.

feedback.explanation_en: Take responsibility for something means accept that it is your duty.

activities.prompt: Before choosing a new club activity, the class should ___ all the available options.

feedback.explanation_en: Consider an option means think carefully about a possible choice.

activities.prompt: What does 'a practical solution' mean in this context? 'Moving the meeting online was a practical solution when the room became unavailable.'

options.text: a workable way to solve the problem

feedback.explanation_en: A practical solution is a workable answer to a problem.

activities.prompt: Which pair of collocations is natural?

options.text: set a goal · meet a deadline
do a goal · catch a deadline
make a goal · arrive a deadline
set a deadline · meet a goal to

feedback.explanation_en: Set a goal and meet a deadline are both standard combinations.

activities.prompt: Complete: After discussing three possible routes, we finally made a ___.

feedback.explanation_en: Make a decision is the standard collocation.

lessons.title: A repair café comes to school
objectives: Identify the main purpose of an informative school text.
Retrieve exact details about arrangements, roles and conditions.
Infer meaning and vocabulary from surrounding evidence.

explanation.en: For a B1 information text, separate the overall purpose from exact details. Names, times, limits and conditions often answer detail questions directly. For inference and vocabulary-in-context, combine nearby clues rather than choosing an answer only because it sounds generally reasonable.
explanation.vi: Với văn bản thông tin B1, cần tách mục đích chung khỏi các chi tiết chính xác như thời gian, vai trò và điều kiện. Với câu suy luận hoặc từ vựng trong ngữ cảnh, hãy kết hợp các dấu hiệu gần đó thay vì chọn đáp án chỉ vì nghe có vẻ hợp lý.

examples: GIST · Why was the notice written?
DETAIL · What must students bring?
INFERENCE · Why is the number of places limited?
VOCABULARY · Use nearby words to infer an unfamiliar phrase.

reading_asset.title: A repair café comes to school
reading_asset.body: Next Wednesday, Green Street Repair Café will run a two-hour session in our school library. The group normally meets once a month at the community centre, where volunteers help people repair small household objects instead of throwing them away. For this school visit, students may bring one broken item such as a desk lamp, a simple toy or a backpack with a damaged zip. Electrical items must be small enough to carry safely, and phones or tablets will not be accepted. The session begins at 3:30 p.m., but students with an item to repair should arrive at 3:15 so a volunteer can check it first. There are only twenty repair places because each volunteer will work with a small group. Students without a broken object may still attend and observe. The organisers will also demonstrate how to sew on a button and replace a bicycle reflector. No previous repair experience is necessary. The aim is not simply to fix objects; the volunteers want students to understand how basic repairs can reduce waste and make useful items last longer. Anyone who wants a repair place must complete the online form by Monday evening. Observers do not need to register.

activities.prompt: What is the main purpose of the text?

options.text: To explain how students can take part in a school repair-café session
To advertise a shop selling new electronic devices
To report the results of a repair competition
To teach students how to repair every household object

feedback.explanation_en: The text explains the event, participation rules, schedule and purpose.

activities.prompt: Where will the school session take place?

feedback.explanation_en: The first sentence states that the school session will be in the school library.

activities.prompt: Which item will NOT be accepted for repair?

options.text: A backpack with a damaged zip

feedback.explanation_en: The text explicitly says that phones or tablets will not be accepted.

activities.prompt: What time should a student with a repair item arrive?

feedback.explanation_en: Students with an item should arrive at 3:15 for the safety check.

activities.prompt: Why are there only twenty repair places?

options.text: Each volunteer will work with a small group.
The library has only twenty chairs.
Only twenty students own broken objects.
The session lasts only twenty minutes.

feedback.explanation_en: The passage gives the small-group volunteer arrangement as the reason for the limit.

activities.prompt: In the sentence 'Students without a broken object may still attend and observe,' what does 'observe' most nearly mean?

options.text: watch what happens without taking a repair place
teach the volunteers how to repair

feedback.explanation_en: The contrast with students who bring repair items shows that observers can attend and watch without using a repair place.

activities.prompt: In the phrase 'make useful items last longer', what does 'last longer' mean?

feedback.explanation_en: The surrounding idea of repair and reducing waste shows that last longer means remain useful for more time.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the volunteers' goal?

options.text: They want students to learn ideas they can use beyond this single event.
They mainly want students to buy replacement parts.
They expect every student to have repair experience.
They want all students to repair phones and tablets.

feedback.explanation_en: The text says the aim is not simply to fix objects but to understand repair and waste reduction.

activities.prompt: Who must complete the online form?

options.text: Students who want a repair place

feedback.explanation_en: The final lines say anyone wanting a repair place must register, while observers do not need to.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer mention sewing on a button and replacing a bicycle reflector?

options.text: To give examples of skills the organisers will demonstrate
To list items students must buy
To explain why the library is closed
To show that only clothing and bicycles can be repaired

feedback.explanation_en: The examples show additional simple repair skills that will be demonstrated.

lessons.title: Should study apps plan every session?
objectives: Identify the writer's balanced main claim in a viewpoint text.
Distinguish supporting details from qualifications and limitations.
Infer the meaning and purpose of language used to qualify a claim.

explanation.en: A B1 viewpoint text may support an idea without presenting it as true in every situation. Look for balancing words such as however, can, may and depends on. Exact detail questions should be answered from the text, while inference questions require combining more than one clue.
explanation.vi: Văn bản nêu quan điểm B1 có thể ủng hộ một ý nhưng vẫn nêu giới hạn. Hãy chú ý các từ như however, can, may và depends on. Câu hỏi chi tiết cần bám sát văn bản; câu suy luận thường phải kết hợp nhiều dấu hiệu.

examples: CLAIM · A tool can help without replacing learner decisions.
QUALIFICATION · However, one plan does not suit every task.
DETAIL · Find what the writer says the app can record.
INFERENCE · Combine examples to understand the writer's attitude.

reading_asset.title: Should study apps plan every session?
reading_asset.body: Study apps can make it easier to organise homework. A learner can record a deadline, divide a large task into smaller steps and receive reminders before work is due. Some apps also show how much time has been spent on different subjects. These features can be useful, especially when several assignments have to be managed at once. However, an app cannot always decide what a learner should do next. A difficult maths problem may need more time than the original plan allowed, while a familiar vocabulary exercise may take less. Learners also differ: one person may work well with frequent reminders, while another may find them distracting. For this reason, a study plan should be treated as a guide rather than a set of fixed instructions. Checking progress is still valuable, but learners need to adjust the plan when the evidence changes. An app can support that process by making deadlines and study patterns visible. The final decision, though, still belongs to the learner.

activities.prompt: Which statement best represents the writer's main view?

options.text: Study apps are useful planning tools, but learners still need to adjust their own plans.
Study apps should make every decision for the learner.
Reminders are harmful for every learner.
Paper plans are always better than digital tools.

feedback.explanation_en: The writer supports study apps as tools but repeatedly limits what they should decide.

activities.prompt: Which feature does the writer say some apps provide?

options.text: A record of time spent on different subjects
Automatic answers to difficult maths questions
A guarantee that homework will be easy

feedback.explanation_en: The first paragraph states that some apps show time spent on different subjects.

activities.prompt: Why might a difficult maths problem change the original plan?

options.text: It may need more time than expected.
Apps do not allow maths homework.
Every learner finishes maths at the same speed.

feedback.explanation_en: The writer directly says a difficult maths problem may need more time than planned.

activities.prompt: What does the text say about reminders?

options.text: They may help one learner but distract another.
They should be sent every five minutes.
They are useful only for vocabulary.

feedback.explanation_en: The passage contrasts learners who benefit from frequent reminders with learners who find them distracting.

activities.prompt: In 'a guide rather than a set of fixed instructions', what does 'fixed' most nearly mean?

feedback.explanation_en: The following sentence says learners need to adjust the plan, so fixed means not changing.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred from the examples of maths and vocabulary tasks?

options.text: Useful plans need to respond to the actual difficulty and time a task requires.
Every subject should receive exactly the same study time.
Vocabulary is always easy and maths is always difficult.
Learners should stop planning before they begin.

feedback.explanation_en: The examples show that actual task demands can differ from an initial estimate.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer use the word 'However' at the start of the second paragraph?

options.text: To introduce a limitation to the benefits described earlier
To repeat the same list of app features
To change the topic to school rules
To prove that apps are useless

feedback.explanation_en: However signals a contrast between the useful features and the limits of automated planning.

activities.prompt: According to the text, what evidence can an app make visible?

options.text: A learner's future exam score with certainty
The correct answer to every task
Whether a teacher likes the learner

feedback.explanation_en: The final paragraph says an app can make deadlines and study patterns visible.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the writer's attitude toward learner independence?

options.text: The writer believes learners should keep responsibility for final decisions.
The writer thinks learners should obey the app without question.
The writer believes planning has no value.
The writer wants apps to remove all learner choices.

feedback.explanation_en: The final sentence explicitly keeps the final decision with the learner, supported by the earlier discussion of adjustment.

activities.prompt: In this text, what does 'adjust the plan' mean?

options.text: change the plan when new information shows it is needed
follow the original plan more strictly

feedback.explanation_en: The surrounding sentences describe changing a plan when task time or learner needs differ from the original expectation.

lessons.title: A school club announcement
objectives: Understand the main purpose of a short school announcement.
Identify simple details such as day, room, time and things to bring.
Follow a simple instruction for new club members.

explanation.en: Listen once to understand the situation. Listen again for simple details such as the day, room number, start time and what students should bring. Do not use the transcript before answering.

objectives: Understand the purpose of a short conversation about a changed plan.
Identify revised times, meeting points and things to bring.

explanation.en: When a plan changes, listen for contrast between the old plan and the new one. Separate the meeting time from the departure time, and notice reasons such as because or so. Listen twice before answering if needed.

audio_asset.source_text: Maya: We need to finish our presentation by Friday. The slides are almost done, but the survey chart is hard to read because I tried to show all sixty responses at once. Could you check it before lunch on Wednesday? Leo: Yes. I have football after school, so morning is better for me. Maya: One more thing. Twelve students skipped one survey question, and I'm worried people will think our data is incomplete. Leo: Add a note explaining that the question was optional. That makes the missing answers clear. lessons.title: Build a clear opinion paragraph
objectives: Analyse an opinion prompt and choose relevant ideas.
Organise an opinion, reason, example and conclusion into a coherent paragraph.
Use suitable linkers, register and language choices before drafting a longer response.

explanation.en: Before writing, identify the exact question and decide your position. Build one clear line of support: opinion → reason → specific example → concluding link. Cohesive words such as because, for example, however and therefore should show a real relationship between ideas, not simply decorate the paragraph. Clear, relevant language is more important than unnecessarily difficult vocabulary.
explanation.vi: Trước khi viết, hãy xác định đúng yêu cầu đề và chọn quan điểm. Xây dựng một mạch rõ ràng: ý kiến → lý do → ví dụ cụ thể → câu kết. Từ nối phải thể hiện quan hệ thật giữa các ý, không chỉ được thêm vào cho có.

examples: OPINION · I think schools should give students one homework-free evening each week.
REASON · This can help students recover and manage other responsibilities.
EXAMPLE · For example, they could use that evening for sport, family time or reading.
CONCLUSION · Therefore, one planned break can support a healthier weekly routine.

lessons.title: Verbs for explaining evidence and change
objectives: Use common B1 verbs for describing evidence, causes and changes.
Distinguish show, suggest and prove according to strength of evidence.
Use cause, lead to, result in, increase, decrease and remain in clear contexts.

explanation.en: When explaining information, choose verbs that match the strength and direction of the evidence. Show can introduce a clear pattern; suggest is more cautious; prove is much stronger and should not be used when the evidence is limited. For change, useful patterns include lead to + noun, result in + noun, cause + noun, increase/decrease, and remain + adjective or noun phrase.
explanation.vi: Khi mô tả bằng chứng, cần chọn động từ đúng mức độ chắc chắn. show có thể nêu một xu hướng rõ; suggest thận trọng hơn; prove rất mạnh. Với thay đổi có thể dùng lead to, result in, cause, increase, decrease, remain.

lessons.title: Why some study breaks work better
objectives: Identify the writer's main claim and supporting contrast.
Distinguish examples from the principle they illustrate.
Infer why timing and break activity both affect concentration.
Interpret cautious language in a balanced advice text.

explanation.en: Advice texts often combine a main principle with examples and limits. At B1, look for contrasts such as in contrast and while, and cautious phrases such as can, may and depends on. These show that the writer is not claiming one rule works for everyone.
explanation.vi: Văn bản lời khuyên thường có nguyên tắc chính, ví dụ và giới hạn. Hãy chú ý các từ nối tương phản như in contrast, while và các từ thận trọng như can, may, depends on.

examples: MAIN CLAIM · A break should help the next work period.
CONTRAST · Stretching creates a pause; a fast social feed may be hard to leave.
LIMIT · The exact pattern is not identical for everyone.
INFERENCE · Combine timing and activity to understand why a break helps or harms focus.

reading_asset.title: Why some study breaks work better
reading_asset.body: Short breaks can help during a long study session, but the effect depends on what a learner does before, during and after the break. A useful break gives attention a chance to reset without making it difficult to return to the task. Standing up, stretching, getting water or looking away from a screen for a few minutes can work well because these activities create a clear pause. In contrast, opening a fast-moving game or social feed may turn a five-minute break into twenty minutes and fill the learner's attention with new information. The timing also matters. Taking a break every few minutes can interrupt concentration before it becomes useful, while working for a very long period without stopping may lead to tired, careless work. A practical approach is to choose a reasonable work block, notice when attention is becoming less effective, and then take a short planned break. The exact pattern will not be identical for everyone. The important point is that a break should support the next period of focused work rather than become a new activity that is hard to leave.

options.text: A good break should make it easier to return to focused work.
Every learner should take a break every five minutes.
Long study sessions should never include breaks.

feedback.explanation_en: The final sentence and earlier examples support the idea that a break should help the next work period.

activities.prompt: Why can stretching or getting water be useful during a break?

options.text: They create a clear pause without adding much new information.
They make the learner finish the whole task immediately.
They replace the need to study.

feedback.explanation_en: The text says these activities let attention reset while keeping the break simple.

activities.prompt: What risk does the writer mention about a fast-moving game or social feed?

options.text: A short break may become much longer and fill attention with new information.
The learner may forget how to use a phone.
The study task may become easier.

feedback.explanation_en: The passage says such activities can extend the break and make returning harder.

activities.prompt: Why might taking breaks every few minutes be unhelpful?

options.text: It can interrupt concentration before a useful period of focus develops.
It means the learner studies for too long.

feedback.explanation_en: The text explicitly says very frequent breaks can interrupt concentration too early.

activities.prompt: What does 'a reasonable work block' mean in context?

options.text: a sensible period of focused work before a break
a fixed rule for every learner

feedback.explanation_en: The phrase refers to a sensible period of work, not an identical fixed duration for everyone.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the writer's view of one universal study schedule?

options.text: The writer does not think one exact schedule suits everyone.
The writer recommends exactly twenty minutes for all learners.
The writer believes timing never matters.
The writer thinks breaks should be random.

feedback.explanation_en: The passage says the exact pattern will not be identical for everyone.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer use 'In contrast'?

options.text: To compare simple reset activities with breaks that may be hard to leave
To introduce a definition of concentration
To change the topic to homework deadlines

feedback.explanation_en: In contrast introduces an opposing type of break activity.

activities.prompt: What does 'depends on' show about the writer's claim?

options.text: The effect changes according to several conditions.
The writer is completely certain about one rule.
The effect is unrelated to learner behaviour.

feedback.explanation_en: Depends on signals that the result varies with conditions.

activities.prompt: Which learner action best follows the writer's advice?

options.text: Work for a planned period, notice falling attention, take a short simple break, then return.
Open a social feed with no time limit whenever work feels difficult.
Take a break after every sentence.
Study for hours without stopping even when making careless mistakes.

feedback.explanation_en: This sequence matches the practical approach described in the passage.

activities.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that break quality matters as well as break length?

options.text: Different break activities can either reset attention or fill it with new information.

feedback.explanation_en: The contrast between simple reset activities and attention-grabbing activities directly supports this idea.

lessons.title: Reply to a message and solve a small problem
objectives: Identify every practical point in a short message task.
Organise a friendly reply that answers questions and proposes a solution.
Use clear time/place language and a suitable closing.
Write an independent response for AI or human review.

explanation.en: A useful A2 reply should answer the exact questions in the message. First underline the practical points: what changed, what the other person needs to know, and what solution you can offer. Then plan a simple order: greeting → answer/update → solution → final question or friendly closing. Keep times and places precise. Do not add private addresses or invented details that the task does not give you.
explanation.vi: Một email A2 cần trả lời đúng từng ý trong tin nhắn. Hãy xác định: điều gì thay đổi, người nhận cần biết gì, và bạn đề xuất giải pháp nào. Sắp xếp: lời chào → thông tin → giải pháp → câu hỏi/lời kết.

examples: TASK · Answer the changed time and suggest a new meeting point.
ORDER · Greeting → update → solution → closing.
PRECISION · 'Meet at the library entrance at 4:15.'
CHECK · Did I answer every practical question?

feedback.explanation_en: Task completion matters more than difficult vocabulary.

objectives: Select relevant comparison criteria from a practical brief.
Compare two options without inventing unsupported facts.
Make a clear recommendation supported by evidence and a limitation.
Use cohesive language and neutral register in an independent response.

explanation.en: A B1 recommendation should not simply list two options. Decide which criteria matter for the reader, compare the options using those criteria, then recommend one. Useful language includes both options…, whereas…, however…, because…, and therefore…. A strong response may acknowledge one disadvantage of the recommended option, but the final choice should remain clear and evidence-based.
explanation.vi: Bài gợi ý B1 cần chọn tiêu chí quan trọng, so sánh hai lựa chọn theo tiêu chí đó rồi đưa ra đề xuất rõ ràng. Có thể nêu một hạn chế của phương án được chọn, nhưng kết luận phải nhất quán và dựa trên dữ kiện.

examples: CRITERIA · time, cost, location, learner needs
COMPARE · Option A is closer, whereas Option B lasts longer.
LIMIT · However, Option A has fewer places.
RECOMMEND · Therefore, I would choose Option A because…

activities.prompt: A task asks you to compare two after-school courses for a friend who has limited time. Which criterion is most relevant?

options.text: The colour of the course poster
The number of letters in the course title

options.text: Course A is shorter, whereas Course B includes an extra weekly session.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence compares the options on duration/frequency.

activities.prompt: Which linker best introduces a disadvantage after a positive point?

feedback.explanation_en: However introduces a contrast or limitation.

activities.prompt: Which recommendation is clearest?

options.text: I would recommend Course A because its shorter schedule fits your available time.
There are courses and they are interesting.

feedback.explanation_en: An effective recommendation selects an option and gives a relevant reason connected to the reader’s needs.

activities.prompt: Which sentence avoids inventing information?

options.text: The brief says Course A costs £20, so I can compare that stated price.

feedback.explanation_en: A recommendation should use stated evidence rather than guesses.

feedback.explanation_en: Neutral wording gives a relevant reason without exaggeration or an insulting tone.

activities.prompt: Which order makes the argument easiest to follow?

options.text: Recommendation → unrelated story → new topic → no conclusion
List of adjectives → greeting → different task

feedback.explanation_en: The sequence builds the recommendation from relevant evidence.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.text: Although Course A is cheaper, Course B offers more practice time.
Although Course A cheaper, but Course B offer more practice time.
Although Course A is cheaper, but Course B offers more practice time.
Course A although is cheaper Course B offering more practice.

feedback.explanation_en: Although introduces the dependent clause without adding but in the main clause.

Course A meets Tuesday for 60 minutes, costs £20 and focuses on conversation. Course B meets Wednesday and Thursday for 90 minutes, costs £25 and focuses on exam reading and writing. Write Alex a recommendation comparing the two courses. lessons.title: A classroom change for Thursday
objectives: Understand the main purpose of a short school announcement.
Identify the day, time, room and materials in the announcement.
Distinguish the changed information from the original plan.

explanation.en: For a short announcement, listen first for the main purpose. On the second listen, note practical details such as day, time, room and what to bring. Words such as now, instead and changed often signal new information.
explanation.vi: Với một thông báo ngắn, lần nghe đầu hãy xác định mục đích chính. Lần nghe thứ hai ghi lại ngày, giờ, phòng và đồ cần mang. Các từ như now, instead, changed thường báo hiệu thông tin mới.

lessons.title: Planning a study-group session
objectives: Identify the main problem and agreed solution in a planning conversation.
Follow details about timing, responsibilities and materials.
Infer why speakers accept or reject suggestions.
Recognise polite intentions such as proposing, checking and clarifying.

explanation.en: In a planning conversation, speakers may suggest several options before agreeing on one. Listen for proposal language such as why don't we, could we and how about, then notice the response and final decision. Separate ideas that are only suggested from plans that are actually agreed.
explanation.vi: Trong hội thoại lập kế hoạch, người nói có thể đưa ra nhiều phương án trước khi chốt. Hãy chú ý các mẫu gợi ý như why don't we, could we, how about, rồi nghe phản hồi và quyết định cuối cùng. Phân biệt ý mới đề xuất với kế hoạch đã được thống nhất.

examples: PROPOSAL · Why don't we meet after lunch?
CHECK · Does 3:30 work for you?
FINAL PLAN · So we will meet in the library at 3:30.
REASON · I cannot stay late because I have practice.

audio_asset.source_text: Nina: We still need to prepare for Friday's history quiz. Shall we meet after school tomorrow? Omar: I can, but I have basketball practice at five, so I need to leave by four thirty. Nina: Then how about meeting in the library at three thirty? We could spend twenty minutes reviewing dates and then practise the longer questions. Omar: That works. I made flashcards for the dates, but I have not finished the chapter summary. Nina: I can bring my summary. Could you bring the teacher's practice sheet? Omar: Yes. Should we invite Maya too? She said she wanted help with the longer answers. Nina: Good idea, but let's message her now so she has time to reply. Omar: One more thing: the library computers are often busy after school. Do we need one? Nina: Probably not. The practice sheet and our notes should be enough. Omar: Great. I'll bring the sheet and flashcards, and you bring the summary. We'll meet by the library entrance at three thirty.

lessons.title: Explain a simple problem and ask for help
objectives: State a simple problem clearly.
Add one useful detail or reason.
Make a polite request for help.
Give a short connected spoken response without reading a full script.

explanation.en: A useful short spoken request has three parts: say the problem, add one important detail, and ask clearly for help. Use simple linking such as because or so. Plan keywords, not a full script, then speak naturally. A text planning note is useful when no microphone is available, but it is not speaking evidence.
explanation.vi: Một lời nhờ giúp ngắn có ba phần: nêu vấn đề, thêm một chi tiết quan trọng và nhờ giúp rõ ràng. Dùng because hoặc so. Chỉ ghi từ khóa thay vì viết cả bài để đọc. Nếu không có micro, ghi chú kế hoạch vẫn hữu ích nhưng không được tính là bằng chứng kỹ năng nói.

examples: PROBLEM · I cannot find Room 18.
DETAIL · My club starts in ten minutes.
REQUEST · Could you show me where it is?
PLAN · problem → detail → polite request

activities.prompt: Which opening states a problem clearly?

options.text: I cannot find the science room.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence directly identifies what the speaker cannot find, so the listener understands the problem.

activities.prompt: Which request is polite and clear?

options.text: Could you show me where Room 18 is?

feedback.explanation_en: Could you...? is a polite and clear request form.

activities.prompt: Which order is easiest for a listener to follow?

feedback.explanation_en: This sequence gives context before the request.

activities.prompt: Which sentence adds a useful reason?

options.text: I need help because my club starts in ten minutes.

feedback.explanation_en: The because-clause clearly explains why the speaker needs help now.

lessons.title: Compare two options and answer a follow-up
objectives: Compare two options using relevant criteria.
State and support a clear preference.
Acknowledge one advantage of the other option.
Respond to a follow-up question without abandoning the main point.

explanation.en: For a B1 comparison, choose two or three useful criteria rather than listing every detail. Compare the options, state your preference and explain why. Acknowledge a strength of the other option if it is relevant. In a follow-up question, respond directly first, then add a reason or example.
explanation.vi: Khi so sánh ở B1, hãy chọn hai hoặc ba tiêu chí quan trọng thay vì liệt kê mọi chi tiết. So sánh, nêu lựa chọn và giải thích lý do. Có thể công nhận một ưu điểm của phương án còn lại. Với câu hỏi phụ, trả lời trực tiếp trước rồi thêm lý do hoặc ví dụ.

examples: COMPARE · Option A is cheaper, whereas Option B gives more practice time.
PREFERENCE · I would choose A because it fits my schedule.
BALANCE · B has one advantage: the sessions are longer.
FOLLOW-UP · If I had more time, I might choose B.

activities.prompt: Which sentence makes a clear comparison?

options.text: The library is quieter, whereas the café stays open later.
The library is a place and the café is a place.

feedback.explanation_en: Whereas clearly contrasts two relevant features.

activities.prompt: Which response gives a preference with a reason?

options.text: I would choose the library because I concentrate better in a quiet place.

feedback.explanation_en: The response states a choice and supports it with a reason.

activities.prompt: Which sentence fairly acknowledges the other option?

options.text: The café is noisier, but it is useful when I need to meet after the library closes.
The café is terrible in every possible way.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence recognises a real advantage while maintaining the comparison.

activities.prompt: Which linker best introduces a contrast?

feedback.explanation_en: However commonly introduces a contrasting point.

options.text: It might be better when I need a later meeting time, because the café stays open longer.
The other option is an option.

feedback.explanation_en: It answers the follow-up directly and gives a reason.

lessons.title: Hear stress in common two-syllable words
objectives: Notice which syllable is stronger in common two-syllable words.
Distinguish first-syllable and second-syllable stress in familiar vocabulary.
Practise stressed words with an audio model before recording.

explanation.en: In a two-syllable word, one syllable is usually stronger. It may be a little louder, longer or clearer. For example, TAble has first-syllable stress, while hoTEL has second-syllable stress. Listen to a real audio model before practising; spelling alone cannot show stress reliably.
explanation.vi: Trong từ hai âm tiết, thường có một âm tiết được nhấn mạnh hơn: có thể to hơn, dài hơn hoặc rõ hơn. Ví dụ TAble nhấn âm đầu, còn hoTEL nhấn âm sau. Cần nghe âm thanh mẫu thật trước khi luyện.

examples: FIRST STRESS · TAble, WINdow, DOCtor
SECOND STRESS · hoTEL, beGIN, reLAX

activities.prompt: Which word has first-syllable stress in standard pronunciation?

feedback.explanation_en: Table normally has stress on the first syllable.

activities.prompt: Which word has second-syllable stress?

feedback.explanation_en: Hotel normally has stress on the second syllable.

activities.prompt: What does the capitalised part show in reLAX?

feedback.explanation_en: The capitalised syllable marks the stronger, stressed syllable.

activities.prompt: Which pair has the same first-syllable stress pattern?

feedback.explanation_en: Both table and window normally have first-syllable stress.

lessons.title: Use sentence stress to show the important idea
objectives: Notice that content words often carry stronger sentence stress.
Use contrastive stress to highlight one corrected or important idea.
Practise short thought groups with an audio model.

explanation.en: English sentence stress helps a listener hear the important information. Content words such as main nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs often receive stronger stress, while many short grammar words are weaker. A speaker can also move strong stress to correct or contrast one idea: I wanted the BLUE notebook, not the red one. Meaning depends on context, so listen to the full model before copying the pattern.
explanation.vi: Trọng âm câu giúp người nghe nhận ra thông tin quan trọng. Danh từ, động từ chính, tính từ và trạng từ thường được nhấn rõ hơn; nhiều từ ngữ pháp ngắn thường nhẹ hơn. Người nói cũng có thể chuyển trọng âm để sửa hoặc đối lập một ý, ví dụ BLUE để đối lập với red.

examples: NEW INFORMATION · I BOUGHT a NEW NOTEBOOK.
CONTRAST · I wanted the BLUE notebook, not the red one.
WHO? · SHE sent the file, not Minh.
THOUGHT GROUP · After lunch / we met in the library.

feedback.explanation_en: Strong stress on BLUE highlights the contrast with red.

activities.prompt: Which type of word often carries important sentence stress?

options.text: Every article such as a or the

feedback.explanation_en: Main content words such as nouns and verbs often carry stronger stress.

feedback.explanation_en: Stressing Mai highlights who did the action.

To make every sentence sound uncertain

feedback.explanation_en: Strong stress on AFTER LUNCH highlights the corrected time.

lessons.title: Introduce yourself and ask a simple question
objectives: Give a short introduction using basic personal information chosen by the learner.
Use a simple greeting and closing.
Ask one clear everyday question.
Speak from keywords instead of reading a full script.

explanation.en: A simple introduction can be short: greeting, your preferred name, one safe detail such as a hobby or favourite school subject, then one question for the other person. You do not need to share private information such as your address, phone number or full legal name. Plan a few keywords and speak naturally.
explanation.vi: Một phần giới thiệu đơn giản có thể rất ngắn: chào hỏi, tên muốn được gọi, một thông tin an toàn như sở thích hoặc môn học yêu thích, rồi hỏi người kia một câu. Không cần chia sẻ địa chỉ, số điện thoại hay họ tên đầy đủ. Chỉ ghi vài từ khóa rồi nói tự nhiên.

examples: GREETING · Hi! I'm Linh.
SAFE DETAIL · I like drawing.
QUESTION · What do you like doing after school?
CLOSING · Nice to meet you.

lessons.title: Explain a problem and propose a practical solution
objectives: Describe a practical problem clearly.
Explain why the problem matters.
Propose a realistic solution and support it with a reason.
Respond to one concern or follow-up question.

explanation.en: For a B1 problem-solution response, make the situation easy to follow: state the problem, explain its effect, suggest a practical solution and give a reason. Then respond directly to one possible concern. You do not need a long speech; clear organisation and specific support matter more.
explanation.vi: Với bài nói B1 dạng vấn đề–giải pháp, hãy nêu vấn đề, giải thích ảnh hưởng, đề xuất một giải pháp thực tế và nêu lý do. Sau đó trả lời trực tiếp một mối lo hoặc câu hỏi phụ. Không cần nói quá dài; bố cục rõ và lý do cụ thể quan trọng hơn.

No problem ever has a difficulty.

feedback.explanation_en: It addresses the concern directly and adjusts the proposal realistically.

lessons.title: Hear the three common -ed endings
objectives: Recognise the common /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/ pronunciations of regular past-tense -ed.
Match familiar regular verbs to the correct ending pattern.
Practise the ending after listening to a real audio model.

explanation.en: Regular past-tense -ed is not always pronounced as a separate syllable. In common standard pronunciation, it can sound like /t/ as in worked, /d/ as in played, or /ɪd/ as in wanted. The spelling stays -ed, but the sound changes according to the final sound of the base verb. Listen to a model before practising.
explanation.vi: Đuôi -ed của động từ quá khứ có ba cách phát âm phổ biến: /t/ như worked, /d/ như played, và /ɪd/ như wanted. Cách viết vẫn là -ed nhưng âm thay đổi theo âm cuối của động từ gốc. Hãy nghe âm thanh mẫu trước khi luyện.

examples: /t/ · worked, watched
/d/ · played, cleaned
/ɪd/ · wanted, needed

activities.prompt: Which word normally ends with the /t/ sound?

feedback.explanation_en: Worked normally ends with /t/.

activities.prompt: Which word normally ends with the /d/ sound?

feedback.explanation_en: Played normally ends with /d/.

activities.prompt: Which word normally has an extra syllable /ɪd/ at the end?

feedback.explanation_en: Wanted is normally pronounced with /ɪd/ as the final syllable.

activities.prompt: Which pair has the same final -ed sound?

feedback.explanation_en: Wanted and needed both normally end with /ɪd/.

activities.prompt: Why can -ed sound different in worked, played and wanted?

options.text: Its pronunciation depends on the final sound of the base verb.
The spelling changes in each word.
The meaning of past tense disappears.

feedback.explanation_en: The ending is pronounced differently according to the sound before it.

lessons.title: Use intonation to ask, check and confirm
objectives: Notice common rising and falling intonation patterns in short questions.
Distinguish a normal information question from a checking or confirming question.
Use intonation to make a short spoken question easier to interpret.

explanation.en: Intonation is the movement of the voice across a phrase. Many ordinary wh- questions use a falling pattern, while yes/no questions often rise. A speaker can also use a rise to check or confirm information. These are common patterns, not rigid rules: context and speaker intention matter. Listen to the full model before copying the pattern.
explanation.vi: Ngữ điệu là sự lên xuống của giọng trong một cụm nói. Nhiều câu hỏi wh- thông thường có xu hướng xuống giọng, còn câu hỏi yes/no thường lên giọng. Người nói cũng có thể lên giọng để kiểm tra hoặc xác nhận thông tin. Đây là xu hướng phổ biến chứ không phải luật tuyệt đối; ngữ cảnh và ý định người nói rất quan trọng.

examples: FALLING · Where is the meeting room?
RISING · Is the meeting at three?
CHECKING · Room fourteen?
CONTEXT · The same words can sound different when the speaker's intention changes.

### AFTER-SCHOOL CLUBS — NEW TERM

**Art Lab — Tuesday, 3:45–4:45**
Try drawing, poster design and simple craft projects. Beginners are welcome. The club provides paper, pencils and paint, but you may bring an old shirt or apron to protect your clothes. There are 16 places, so sign up by Monday lunchtime.

reading_asset.title: CAN SHORT BREAKS HELP YOU LEARN?
reading_asset.body:
### CAN SHORT BREAKS HELP YOU LEARN?

When people study for a long time, they sometimes notice that they are still looking at the page but no longer thinking carefully about it. A short, planned break can help at this point. Standing up, stretching, getting some water or looking away from a screen for a few minutes may help a learner return with better attention.

However, this does not mean that every interruption is useful. A break can easily become much longer than planned. For example, checking one message on a phone may lead to ten minutes of videos or group-chat replies. In that case, the learner may find it harder to return to the original task.

One useful approach is to decide on a clear stopping point before beginning a study session. A learner might work until the end of a short section, then take a five-minute break. The exact timing does not need to be the same for everyone. A difficult maths problem may require a longer period of concentration, while reviewing vocabulary might work well in shorter blocks.

The important point is that breaks should support the task rather than replace it. If a learner notices attention beginning to drift, a brief planned pause may be useful. But if the learner is deeply focused and making progress, there may be no reason to stop simply because a timer says so.

lessons.title: What We Learned from a Pop-Up Sale

audio_asset.source_text: Last month, our class organised a one-day pop-up sale to raise money for new sports equipment. At first, we planned to sell only homemade snacks. However, a survey showed that many students wanted second-hand books as well, so we added a book table. On the morning of the event, we discovered that the room was smaller than we had expected. We moved the snack table outside, where more people could see it. By lunchtime, most of the books had sold, but the snacks were selling slowly. Instead of lowering every price, we offered a small discount on snack boxes bought by families. That helped, and we reached our fundraising target just before closing. The most useful lesson wasn't about money. We learned to ask people what they wanted, respond calmly when plans changed, and keep simple records. Next time, we'll check the room size before making the layout.

lessons.title: Checking a Photo Before Sharing

audio_asset.source_text:
A: Someone posted a photograph of the river near our town. The water looks bright green. People are saying a factory must be putting chemicals into it.
B: That's worrying, but do we know when the picture was taken?
A: No. The post doesn't give a date. It just says, "Look what happened today."
B: Could the colour be caused by the camera or by something natural? We shouldn't guess from one photograph.
A: You're right. I nearly shared it because the comments sounded so certain.
B: Let's check whether the local environmental office has reported anything. We could also look for a second photograph from a reliable source.
A: I've found a notice from last year about harmless green dye used to test the movement of water. But that doesn't prove this is the same situation.
B: Exactly. It gives us another possibility, not a final answer.
A: I'll wait for a current official update instead of spreading the claim. If there's a real problem, we can share confirmed information and ask what people should do.
B: Good plan. Being careful isn't the same as ignoring the problem.

lessons.title: Read the task before writing
objectives: Identify the writer’s topic and purpose in a short task.
List two to three compulsory content points without inventing extra requirements.
Notice the reader, length and tone before drafting.

explanation.en:
Use four boxes. TOPIC names what the writing is about. TASK tells you the action (invite, explain, request, recommend). MUST INCLUDE lists each detail you have to cover. BOUNDARY names the reader, tone and any word/format limit. Read the task twice: once for purpose, once to tick each requirement. Do not treat background details as instructions.

Typical mistake and correction: Common mistake: adding an invented fee or missing one required detail because it appeared in the middle of the instructions. Repair: mark each Must Include point and tick it before submission.

examples: MODEL CONTEXT · Independent worked demo — A youth centre newsletter asks: “Write a short notice inviting students to a free astronomy evening. Say WHEN it begins (Friday, 5:30 p.m.), WHERE to meet (community hall), and WHAT to bring (a notebook). Use a friendly tone. Write 50–70 words.”

TEACHER THINKING · TOPIC = astronomy evening; TASK = invite students; MUST INCLUDE = Friday 5:30, community hall, notebook; BOUNDARY = students, friendly notice, 50–70 words. The newsletter does NOT request a ticket price or contact number. Outline: invitation → time/place → what to bring → welcome.

WORKED MODEL · Join our free astronomy evening this Friday at 5:30 p.m. We will meet at the community hall and learn to recognise some bright stars. Please bring a notebook to write down interesting things you notice. Everyone is welcome, including beginners. We hope to see you there! Please arrive a few minutes early so we can begin together.
WHY THIS MODEL WORKS · The model answers every requested practical point, keeps the friendly notice format and avoids unsupported information. It is NOT a model answer for the independent task below.

activities.prompt: A task says: “Tell a new classmate about the lunchtime drawing club.” What is the TOPIC?

feedback.explanation_en: The topic is the drawing club, not the action or an unrelated school activity. Next step: Do not confuse the reader with the topic.

activities.prompt: A task says: “Write a message asking a friend to help carry books.” What is the TASK?

options.text: Write a report to the school

feedback.explanation_en: “Asking” is the requested writing action. Next step: Identify the action verb in the instructions.

activities.prompt: A club asks for a reply including the event day, room and one item to bring. What is compulsory?

options.text: A long story about last year

feedback.explanation_en: All three details are required; other material cannot replace them. Next step: Count all specified requirements.

activities.prompt: The reader is a close friend and the task says “friendly text message.” Which opening fits?

options.text: Hi Noor, are you free on Saturday?

feedback.explanation_en: The greeting matches a friend and a short, informal message. Next step: Check the audience before choosing the tone.

activities.prompt: A notice task says “Write 60–80 words.” Which statement is correct?

options.text: The range is a boundary, not an automatic writing-quality score.
Exactly 80 words always earns full marks.
Longer writing is necessarily more accurate.

feedback.explanation_en: Length guides the task format; it cannot measure quality by itself. Next step: Do not turn length guidance into a proficiency score.

activities.prompt: A message task provides a meeting time and place. Which note is most useful before writing?

options.text: What to say → confirmed time → confirmed place → friendly end
Write only the greeting and hope for the best.
Add an invented price to make it interesting.

feedback.explanation_en: The brief outline protects the two required practical points. Next step: An outline should follow the actual prompt.

activities.prompt: Before sending a reply, which self-check matters most?

options.text: Did I use five difficult adjectives?
Did I exceed the maximum word limit?
Can I tick every compulsory point in the question?
Did I add unrelated information to sound clever?

feedback.explanation_en: Matching each requirement to an actual part of the draft checks task completion. Next step: Highlight where you answered each requirement.

activities.prompt: Independent writing, distinct prompt: A friend named Maya wants information about your school's weekend birdwatching group. Write Maya a friendly message explaining WHAT the group does, WHEN it meets (Saturday, 9:00 a.m.), WHERE students meet (school garden gate), and WHAT to bring (a pencil). Ask if Maya would like to join. Aim for 70–100 words. Do not give private addresses, phone numbers or invented prices.

lessons.title: Brainstorm ideas that answer the question
objectives: Generate several possible ideas without drafting full paragraphs.
Reject ideas that do not answer the actual prompt.
Select two workable ideas and connect each to a clear reason.

explanation.en:
Write the exact task at the top. Brainstorm 4–5 short ideas; do not judge them immediately. Then test each idea: Does it answer the prompt? Can I explain WHY it helps? Is it realistic in this context? Keep the best two, not all five. Turn each into an IDEA → REASON pair. Personal facts and invented statistics are not needed.

Typical mistake and correction: Common mistake: collecting many impressive-sounding ideas that do not answer the question. Repair: cross out one off-topic item and replace it with an IDEA → REASON pair.

examples: MODEL CONTEXT · Independent worked demo — “Suggest two rainy-day activities for a school club and explain why they are suitable indoors.” Brainstorm: board games; short play rehearsal; outdoor football; baking with hot ovens; quiz. Reject football (not indoor) and baking (extra safety/equipment demands).

TEACHER THINKING · Keep IDEA 1 = board games; REASON = groups can play without going outside. IDEA 2 = short play rehearsal; REASON = everyone can take a role even if it rains. Outline: suggestion → board games + why → rehearsal + why → polite close.

WORKED MODEL · For rainy days, our club could organise board games in the classroom. Small groups could play together, so no one needs to go outside. We could also rehearse a short play. Every member could choose a role, and we would use a room that is already available. Both activities would give us something enjoyable to do indoors.
WHY THIS MODEL WORKS · The two selected actions fit the indoor requirement and each has a plausible reason. The demo does not give the answers to the independent task.

activities.prompt: A prompt asks for ways to make a classroom quieter. Which idea is directly relevant?

options.text: Give groups a clear indoor voice-level reminder.

feedback.explanation_en: An indoor reminder addresses noise inside the classroom. Next step: Choose ideas that change the named situation.

activities.prompt: Which is a useful reason for placing labelled recycling bins near classrooms?

options.text: So students can sort paper and plastic more easily.
So nobody ever needs a lesson.

feedback.explanation_en: The reason explains how the action can help; it is not just a repeated noun. Next step: Ask how or why the proposed action helps.

activities.prompt: A brainstorm includes four ideas. When should you choose the final two?

options.text: After checking relevance and explaining the likely benefit
Only after writing a complete essay

feedback.explanation_en: Selection follows idea generation and a relevance test. Next step: Brainstorm first, filter second.

activities.prompt: A prompt asks for two safe outdoor lunchtime activities. Which should be rejected?

options.text: A playground ball game with rules
Watching a film in a dark indoor cinema

feedback.explanation_en: The cinema activity does not satisfy the outdoor boundary. Next step: Check boundary conditions in the task.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows an idea followed by a useful reason?

options.text: Put signs by the taps → this can remind pupils to turn off water.
Put signs by the taps → signs are signs.
Put signs by the taps → I like everything.
Put signs by the taps → the school is old.

feedback.explanation_en: The reason identifies the reminder mechanism and matches the proposed action. Next step: Reason should connect causally to the idea.

activities.prompt: A student writes “We should organise a reading circle because it would help us share book recommendations.” Which statement is best?

options.text: It explains a relevant idea with a realistic benefit.
It is off-topic in any situation.

feedback.explanation_en: The sentence links a suggestion to a reason; proficiency depends on the full task and assessment. Next step: Do not infer CEFR from one good sentence.

activities.prompt: Which revision is most useful when a draft has four ideas but explains none?

options.text: Replace every word with a longer synonym.
Keep the best two ideas and explain a benefit for each.

feedback.explanation_en: Fewer developed ideas communicate more than an unsupported list. Next step: Choose depth and relevance over sheer count.

activities.prompt: Independent writing: Your school library asks students how to make the library more welcoming at break time. Suggest TWO realistic changes, explain why each would help students, and finish with a friendly recommendation. Aim for 80–110 words. Use no invented survey data or private student details.
